note: Weighted toward what 2026 interviews actually probe -- cost reasoning, failure recovery, operational maturity -- rather than raw scalability. `trap` is the specific omission that sinks candidates: naming a technology without naming the decision it forces.

cards.name: Caching and eviction
cards.prompt: You propose Redis in front of the database. What must you specify before that is a real answer?
must_cover: cache-aside vs read-through -- cache-aside is the common pattern and puts invalidation on you
eviction policy (LRU / LFU / TTL) and WHY that one for this access pattern
the cache-aside stale-entry race: a read miss interleaved with a write can cache a stale value PERMANENTLY -- fixed by delete-on-write plus short TTL, or versioned keys
what happens on a miss -- thundering herd, and single-flight or request coalescing
memory sizing, what gets evicted first when it fills, and cold-start after a failover
cards.trap: Saying 'add Redis' and stopping. The interviewer is waiting for eviction policy and invalidation; without them you have proposed an unbounded memory leak with a stale-data bug.

cards.name: Log/queue ordering and delivery
cards.prompt: You put Kafka between two services. What ordering and delivery guarantees have you actually bought?
must_cover: ordering is per-partition only -- so the partition key IS the ordering decision

since Kafka 3.0 the Java producer is idempotent by default (acks=all), so producer-level dedup is already on; end-to-end exactly-once still needs transactions plus isolation.level=read_committed, costs throughput, and holds only INSIDE Kafka -- never for external side effects
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection > 1 with retries reorders messages unless idempotence is enabled -- the gotcha that ties ordering and delivery together
consumer rebalance: in-flight messages, partition reassignment, duplicate delivery
consumer lag as the health metric, and what you do when it grows
retention: what happens when a consumer is down longer than the retention window
cards.trap: Claiming 'Kafka gives ordering' with no partition-key discussion. Global ordering across partitions does not exist, and choosing a key with skew silently creates a hot partition.

cards.name: Sharding and rebalancing
cards.prompt: You shard the database. How do you add shard N+1 two years later?
must_cover: shard key choice and the queries it makes expensive (cross-shard joins, fan-out reads)
consistent hashing / virtual nodes vs modulo -- modulo remaps everything on resize
the migration itself: dual-write, backfill, verify, cut over, with rollback at each step
hot shards from skewed keys, and what you do about a celebrity tenant
transactions that span shards, and whether you avoid them or run 2PC
cards.trap: Sharding by modulo and never discussing resize. 'We'll shard by user_id % N' is fine until N changes and every key moves.

cards.name: Consistency models
cards.prompt: Where in your design is eventual consistency acceptable, and where is it a bug?
must_cover: name the MODEL: linearizable, sequential, causal, eventual -- and separately the SESSION guarantees, which are a different axis: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes
monotonic reads is the anomaly users actually report -- time running backward as successive requests hit different replicas
transaction isolation is a THIRD axis, not the same question: read committed / repeatable read / snapshot isolation / serializable, and write skew as the anomaly SI still permits
read-your-writes for the user's own edits -- usually non-negotiable
cost: linearizability requires coordination, so latency and availability under partition (PACELC, not just CAP)
cards.trap: Saying 'eventually consistent' as if it were one guarantee, and conflating replication consistency with transaction isolation. The follow-up is always 'what can a user actually observe', which requires naming the anomaly.

cards.name: Idempotency and retries
cards.prompt: A payment request times out. The client retries. What stops a double charge?
must_cover: idempotency key supplied by the client, stored with the result
how long you retain keys, and what a replay after expiry does
the write must be atomic with recording the key -- otherwise the crash window reintroduces the bug

the concurrency window, not just the crash window: two retries in flight at once. Insert the key in a PENDING state behind a uniqueness constraint so the loser blocks or gets in-flight status -- a plain check-then-act still double-charges
distinguishing retry from a genuine second request
retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter, and a budget so retries cannot amplify an outage
cards.trap: Retries without idempotency keys. Also: retry storms -- naive retry turns a partial outage into a total one.

cards.name: Observability cost
cards.prompt: Your observability bill is now 15% of infrastructure spend and growing 40% a year. What is driving it and what do you cut?
must_cover: unbounded label cardinality is the dominant driver -- one user_id label multiplies series count by your user count; metrics are cheap per point and expensive per SERIES
the three signals have different cost profiles: metrics cheap, logs expensive, traces expensive but samplable

tail sampling costs more because you must ingest, route all spans of a trace to one collector, and buffer 100% of them until the trace completes before deciding -- it moves cost from backend storage to collector memory and network
retention tiering: hot for days, cold/archived for compliance
what you lose with each cut, stated honestly
cards.trap: Proposing 'more dashboards' as the answer to an incident. Observability has a budget.

cards.name: Failure domains and blast radius
cards.prompt: A dependency you call on every request starts returning 500s. Walk through what happens.
must_cover: timeouts on every network call, and a budget that shrinks down the call chain
circuit breaker: thresholds, half-open probing, what the fallback returns
bulkheads -- separate pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads/connections
graceful degradation: which features turn off first and who decided that
cascading failure: retries plus no backoff turns a blip into an outage
cards.trap: Assuming dependencies fail cleanly and fast. The dangerous case is slow, not down -- a dependency at p99=30s exhausts your connection pool while every health check stays green.

cards.name: Rate limiting
cards.prompt: Design rate limiting for a public API. What algorithm and where does the state live?
must_cover: token bucket vs leaky bucket vs sliding window log vs sliding window counter, and the tradeoff
distributed state: per-node approximation vs a shared store, and the latency that adds
what the client sees -- 429 with Retry-After, and headers describing remaining quota
limiting dimension: per-user, per-IP, per-endpoint, per-tenant
fail-open vs fail-closed when the limiter store is unreachable
cards.trap: Fixed windows allow 2x burst at the boundary. Also: not answering what happens when the rate-limit store itself is down.

cards.name: Replication and failover
cards.prompt: Your primary database fails. Describe the next 60 seconds.
must_cover: sync vs async replication, and the data loss window (RPO) each implies
how failover is triggered -- automatic with a quorum, or human
split brain, and the fencing that prevents two primaries accepting writes
replica lag: reads served from a lagging replica after failover
RTO vs RPO stated as numbers, not adjectives
cards.trap: Automatic failover without fencing. Two primaries is worse than being down, and the interviewer will ask about it.

cards.name: Zero-downtime schema change
cards.prompt: Rename a column on a 500M-row table with no downtime.
must_cover: expand-migrate-contract: add new, dual-write, backfill in batches, read from new, drop old
each step deployable and reversible independently
backfill throttling so it does not saturate IO or replication
locking behavior of the specific DDL on the specific engine -- some ALTERs rewrite the whole table
the deploy is now multiple releases, and old and new code run simultaneously
cards.trap: Treating the migration as one step. Also: forgetting that during the rollout, old and new application code both run against the same schema.

cards.name: Backpressure and load shedding
cards.prompt: Traffic is 5x your capacity. What does the system do?
must_cover: shed early and cheaply -- at the edge, before expensive work
priority: which requests are dropped first, and who decided
queue depth as the signal, and why unbounded queues are a latency bomb
propagating backpressure upstream rather than buffering silently
admission control vs autoscaling, and why autoscaling is too slow for a spike
cards.trap: Assuming autoscaling absorbs it. Scale-up takes minutes; the spike is now. Unbounded queues 'accept' everything and then time out anyway, having done all the work.

cards.name: Cost reasoning
cards.prompt: Your design works. What does it cost per month, and what is the biggest line item?
must_cover: estimate the dominant cost: usually egress, storage growth, or always-on compute
cross-AZ and egress traffic -- frequently the surprise line item
NAT gateway data-processing charges, which routinely exceed cross-AZ transfer and are the most commonly missed line item
storage growth rate and retention policy, because storage only accumulates
reserved/spot vs on-demand, and the availability tradeoff
cost per unit of business value (per user, per request), not just total
cards.trap: Not costing the design at all. 'it scales' without 'and here is what it costs' is an incomplete answer, and cross-AZ traffic is the most common blind spot.

cards.name: Search and inverted indexes
cards.prompt: Add full-text search over 100M documents.
must_cover: inverted index structure; why LIKE '%x%' cannot work at this size
indexing pipeline: near-real-time vs batch, and the visibility lag users see
relevance scoring (BM25) and that ranking quality is the actual product
sharding the index and scatter-gather query cost
reindexing without downtime when the analyzer or mapping changes
cards.trap: Proposing Elasticsearch without discussing the indexing lag or what happens during a full reindex.

cards.name: Multi-region
cards.prompt: Users in the EU report 400ms latency. You are single-region in us-east. What now?
must_cover: read replicas near users vs full active-active, and the enormous difference in complexity
write path: still cross-region, or partitioned by region?
conflict resolution if writes are accepted in two places -- LWW loses data, CRDTs constrain the data model
data residency (GDPR) may force partitioning regardless of latency
cross-region replication cost and lag
cards.trap: Jumping to active-active. But also: read replicas break read-your-writes -- the user writes to us-east, reads the EU replica, and their own edit is gone. Sticky routing for a lag window is the fix, and saying so is what makes 'just add replicas' a real answer.

cards.name: Queue vs stream
cards.prompt: When do you use SQS-style queueing rather than a Kafka-style log?
must_cover: queue: work distribution, per-message ack, deletion after consumption, easy competing consumers
SQS standard is UNORDERED and at-least-once; FIFO queues order per message group at much lower throughput. That, not replay, is usually the real deciding factor
log: replayable, multiple independent consumers, ordered per partition, retention-based
replay requirement is usually the deciding question
DLQ handling and poison-message policy in both
operational weight: managed queue is far cheaper to run than a log
cards.trap: Defaulting to Kafka for everything. If you never replay and have one consumer group, you have bought operational burden for nothing.

cards.name: Sessions vs tokens
cards.prompt: Stateless JWTs or server-side sessions?
must_cover: JWT revocation is the core problem -- you cannot un-issue a token before expiry, so you keep a jti denylist until expiry, which reintroduces exactly the server state JWTs were meant to avoid; the practical answer is short TTLs plus a small denylist
alg=none and algorithm-confusion (RS256 key used as an HS256 secret) -- pin the expected algorithm, never trust the header
short-lived access + refresh token, refresh rotation with reuse detection, and where the refresh token lives
session store lookup cost vs the revocation ability it buys
key rotation and how verifiers learn new keys
where tokens are stored client-side, and the XSS/CSRF tradeoff
cards.trap: Choosing JWTs for statelessness and having no revocation answer. 'Logout' and 'ban this user' both require it.

cards.name: Hot keys and skew
cards.prompt: One tenant is 40% of your traffic. What breaks?
must_cover: hot partition/shard, and why more capacity does not help a single key
key splitting/salting, and the read-side fan-out it forces
read hot keys and write hot keys need different fixes: salting/splitting is a WRITE-path fix; for reads you replicate the key or put a short-TTL near-cache in front with request coalescing
per-tenant quotas and isolation so one tenant cannot starve others
dedicated infrastructure for outlier tenants
detecting skew before it pages you -- per-key metrics, not just aggregates
cards.trap: Assuming uniform distribution. Real workloads are Zipfian, and aggregate dashboards hide a single key saturating one node.

cards.name: How to open a design interview
cards.prompt: "Design a URL shortener." You have 45 minutes. What are the first ten of them?
must_cover: clarify scope before designing: who uses it, read/write ratio, is it public, what is explicitly OUT of scope
functional requirements as a short list, then non-functional (latency target, availability target, consistency needs, retention)
back-of-envelope: QPS from DAU x actions/day / 86400, peak as ~2-3x average, storage as rows x bytes x retention, bandwidth as QPS x payload
the API sketch -- a handful of endpoints with their request/response shapes
the data model and the ACCESS PATTERNS it must serve, before choosing a datastore
only then the high-level diagram, and state where you will go deep
cards.trap: Diagramming boxes in minute two. Every other card in this deck is a minute-30 follow-up; this is the part that decides whether you get there. Skipping the estimate means every later capacity claim is unsupported.

cards.name: API design and pagination
cards.prompt: Design a list endpoint over a table that grows to 100M rows.
must_cover: cursor (keyset) pagination over OFFSET -- OFFSET n scans and discards n rows, so deep pages get linearly slower
OFFSET also skips or duplicates rows when the underlying set changes between requests
the cursor must be an opaque, stable, tie-broken sort key (e.g. created_at + id)
page size limits, and a hard cap the client cannot override
versioning and how you deprecate a field without breaking existing clients
cards.trap: Offering `?page=5000&per_page=100` and not knowing why it is slow. This gets asked constantly and the OFFSET answer is treated as a red flag.

cards.name: Operational maturity
cards.prompt: The design is done. How do you deploy and operate it?
must_cover: deploy strategy: canary or blue-green, and the automated rollback trigger
feature flags decouple deploy from release -- the most important modern answer, and separate from canary/blue-green
SLO with an error budget, and what the budget being spent actually changes
the alerts you would page on -- symptoms users feel, not causes
runbook for the top two failure modes
what you would test in a game day / failure injection
cards.trap: Ending at the architecture diagram. 2026 interviews explicitly probe operational maturity, and 'how do you know it is broken' is a standard follow-up.

cards.name: Dual writes and the outbox
cards.prompt: You write to Postgres and publish to Kafka. How do you make those atomic?
must_cover: you cannot atomically write two systems -- either can fail after the other succeeds
transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox TABLE in the same transaction as the business row, then a relay publishes it
change data capture (Debezium) reading the WAL as the relay, and why that beats polling
the relay is at-least-once, so consumers still need idempotency or dedup on event id
sagas with compensating actions when the work genuinely spans services and 2PC is off the table
cards.trap: 'Write to the DB, then publish.' If the process dies between them the event is lost forever and nothing detects it. This is the most common distributed-data bug in practice and it gets asked directly.
